lesson.title: Differentiating What You Cannot Integrate
lesson.summary: FTC part one is also a computational shortcut: to differentiate an accumulation function you never need to actually evaluate the integral, you just plug the upper limit into the integrand, which matters enormously when no elementary antiderivative exists at all.
lesson.body:
FTC part one states that if F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F'(x) = f(x). Treated purely as a computational rule rather than a conceptual statement, this says something quite practical: to differentiate an accumulation function, you do not need to find an explicit formula for the integral at all. You do not antidifferentiate f, plug in x, plug in a, and subtract, only to then differentiate the result and watch it collapse back to f(x), undoing all that work. You simply evaluate the integrand itself at the upper limit, and you are done.

This shortcut is not just a convenience for saving algebra on functions you could integrate anyway. It is essential for functions you cannot integrate in closed form at all. Many perfectly respectable, continuous functions, functions built from polynomials, exponentials, and trigonometric functions using ordinary combinations of addition, multiplication, and composition, simply do not have antiderivatives that can be written down using those same building blocks. FTC part one guarantees that an antiderivative still exists, namely the accumulation function itself, and it hands you that antiderivative's derivative directly, without ever requiring you to name the antiderivative explicitly.

Here is the classic worked example. Let F(x) = the integral from 1 to x of the square root of (1 + t^3) dt. The integrand, the square root of 1 + t^3, has no elementary antiderivative, meaning there is no finite combination of familiar functions whose derivative equals it exactly. That would seem to make F impossible to work with, but FTC part one differentiates it immediately: F'(x) = the square root of (1 + x^3). You never had to know a formula for F(x) itself. Plugging in a specific value confirms the arithmetic: F'(2) = the square root of (1 + 2^3) = the square root of (1 + 8) = the square root of 9 = 3. Also note F(1) = 0 trivially, since the integral from 1 to 1 of anything is 0, the interval has collapsed to a single point with no width to accumulate over.

This is FTC part one at its most powerful: a theorem that lets you differentiate a function you could never write down explicitly, simply by reading off the integrand at the upper limit. The final chapter in this sequence pushes this one step further, asking what happens when that upper limit is not just x itself but some other function of x.
